title: Custom Interval
statement:
Write two functions that work like `setInterval` and `clearInterval`, except that the pause between calls grows steadily:

- `customInterval(fn, delay, period)` starts calling `fn` over and over and returns a number `id` that names this repetition. Count the calls of `fn` from `0`. Call number `count` happens `delay + period * count` ms after the previous call; for call `0` that wait is just `delay`, measured from the moment `customInterval` was called.
- `customClearInterval(id)` stops the repetition named `id`: `fn` is not called by it any more.

Each case gives `delay`, `period` and `stopTime`. The judge calls `customInterval(fn, delay, period)` at time `0` and `customClearInterval(id)` at `stopTime` ms, with the `id` it got back. The answer is the list of times, in ms from the start, at which `fn` ran. `stopTime` never falls exactly on a moment when `fn` is due.
constraints: stopTime is not a time at which fn is due to run
signature: int[] customInterval(int delay, int period, int stopTime)
api: customInterval(fn: () => void, delay: number, period: number): number; customClearInterval(id: number): void
notes:
## Intuition

`setInterval` waits the same time between calls, but here every wait is `period` ms longer than the last, so no single interval fits. Instead, chain one `setTimeout` after another: each run of `fn` schedules the next run with the next, longer wait. That raises a second problem. Every link of the chain has a new timer handle, yet the caller holds one `id` for the whole repetition. So hand out a stable `id` and keep a map from it to whichever timer is pending right now; clearing looks up that timer and cancels it. (The brute force schedules sixty runs up front at their absolute times and cancels all that remain; it works for this window but wastes timers and needs an arbitrary cap.)

## Approach

1. Keep `schedules`, a `Map` from each `id` to its pending timer, and a counter `nextId` for fresh ids.
2. In `customInterval`, take a new `id` and start `count` at `0`.
3. `scheduleNext` computes `wait = delay + period * count`, sets a timer for it, and records the timer under `id`.
4. When the timer fires, call `fn`, increase `count`, and call `scheduleNext` again for the following run.
5. Call `scheduleNext` once to start the chain, and return `id`.
6. `customClearInterval(id)` cancels the timer stored under `id` and forgets it.

## Example 1, step by step

`delay = 50`, `period = 20`, `stopTime = 225`.

- 0 ms: `id = 0`, `count = 0`, `wait = 50`, so a timer is set for 50 ms.
- 50 ms: `fn` runs; `count = 1`, `wait = 70`, next timer at 120 ms.
- 120 ms: `fn` runs; `count = 2`, `wait = 90`, next timer at 210 ms.
- 210 ms: `fn` runs; `count = 3`, `wait = 110`, next timer at 320 ms.
- 225 ms: `customClearInterval(0)` cancels the timer due at 320 ms.

The answer is `[50, 120, 210]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) per run of `fn` and per clear.
- Space: O(1) per active repetition: one map entry holding its pending timer.

## Pitfalls

- Returning the first timer's handle as the id: by the time the clear comes, a later timer is pending, and cancelling the first one does nothing.
- Measuring every wait from time 0 (runs at 50, 70, 90) instead of from the previous run (50, 120, 210).
- Increasing `count` before the first wait, which makes the first run come at `delay + period` instead of `delay`.
- One shared timer variable for all repetitions: a second `customInterval` would overwrite it, and clearing one would stop the other.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `schedules` | map from each id to the timer currently pending for it |
| `nextId` | the id the next `customInterval` call hands out |
| `id` | the stable name of one repetition |
| `count` | how many times `fn` has run in this repetition |
| `wait` | the pause before the next run, `delay + period * count` |
| `timer` | the handle of the pending `setTimeout` |

narration.1: schedules maps each repetition id to the timer that is pending for it right now.
narration.2: nextId hands out a fresh id for every customInterval call.
narration.5: Take a stable id for this repetition; it stays the same while the timers change.
narration.6: count is how many times fn has run so far, starting at 0.
narration.8: The next pause grows with count: delay for the first run, then period ms more each time.
narration.9: Schedule the next run after that pause.
narration.10: When the timer fires, run fn.
narration.11: One more run is done, so the next pause will be longer.
narration.12: Chain the following run from this moment.
narration.14: Remember the pending timer under the id so a clear can find it.
narration.16: Start the chain with the first wait of delay ms.
narration.17: Return the id the caller will pass to customClearInterval.
narration.21: Cancel whichever timer is pending for this id, so fn never runs again.
narration.22: Forget the id; its repetition is over.
